title: The Monk Who Never Left: Figure and Truth at Corbie, and the Question of the Dog-Headed Men
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Picardy, a birth no one records
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no source names the year or the place, and the range c. 800-805 is inferred backward from his teaching career
stops.campa: No vita is written for him. No charter names his parents, no obit gives his year, no village claims him. Historians work backward from the years he is known to be teaching and arguing, and set his birth somewhere in Picardy in the first years of the ninth century. The country is flat and wet, cut by the Somme, thick with Benedictine houses. Whatever happens before the abbey gate is missing from the record, and nothing later fills it in. Who taught him his Latin, and where, no source says.
suggested_refs: The Picard countryside around Corbie, in which no source places his birth

stops.name: Corbie, the habit taken
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the entry is undated and is placed in the 820s by inference from his later career
stops.campa: The abbey was founded in 661 by the queen Balthild and Clotaire III and colonized with monks out of Luxeuil, and by the ninth century it holds some three hundred men. Adalard, a cousin of the emperor, has raised it into one of the schools of the Frankish world; Wala has governed it after him. Ratramnus takes the Benedictine habit here as a young man. No source places him outside the enclosure again in sixty years of documented life. The Rule is read aloud in chapter every morning; the bell divides the day into hours.
suggested_refs: The abbey church of Corbie, whose portal and western towers still stand

stops.name: Corbie, the scriptorium and the new hand
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the Corbie hand is dated by surviving manuscripts, not by his presence at any desk
stops.campa: The workshop at Corbie is one of the great manuscript shops of the age, credited with helping fix the clear round minuscule that will carry Latin across Europe and come back, centuries later, as the shape of printed type. Ratramnus is formed inside this book culture and will use it: everything he writes leaves the abbey first as a physical object, sewn and bound, before it leaves as an argument anyone can answer. Ruled parchment, cut quills, one monk reading aloud to a row of copyists.
suggested_refs: Carolingian minuscule as developed in the Corbie scriptorium

stops.name: Corbie, the library that reads Africa and Spain
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no catalogue entry ties either book to his hand, though both circulate widely in Carolingian houses and Corbie's library is documented as unusually wide
stops.campa: The library is assembled from as far away as Italy, and two books in it will decide the last argument of his life. Augustine, writing at Hippo four centuries earlier, ruled in the sixteenth book of the City of God that whatever is rational and mortal descends from Adam, whatever shape its body takes. Isidore of Seville, in the Etymologies, catalogued the dog-headed men among the monstrous races: born in India, and their barking confesses them beasts rather than men. Both sit on the same shelf.
suggested_refs: Augustine, De Civitate Dei XVI.8
Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae XI.3.15
sources: Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, chapter 8
Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae, Book XI.3

stops.name: Corbie, Paschasius writes on the body and blood
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 831-833, with a later revision dedicated to the king
stops.campa: A fellow monk of the house, Paschasius Radbertus, writes the first sustained Latin treatise on the Eucharist. His answer is unambiguous: the bread and wine on the altar become, really and substantially, the flesh born of Mary and crucified at Calvary, that same body and not a likeness of it. He will revise the book later and dedicate the revision to the king. For a decade nobody at Corbie contradicts him in writing. Ratramnus is in the same choir every day of that decade and puts nothing on parchment against him.
suggested_refs: Paschasius Radbertus, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini

stops.name: Corbie, Paschasius is elected abbot
stops.date_confidence: attested: 843, per the abbey's list of abbots, which gives him 843-851
stops.campa: Paschasius succeeds Isaac and takes the abbacy. Ratramnus stays, under obedience to a man whose central book he is about to take apart, and there is no sign that either of them treats this as a scandal. The house runs as houses run: fields, school, scriptorium, the sick, the guests at the gate. Willemien Otten will argue eleven centuries later that the quarrel between these two was assembled by historians, since neither monk ever names or quotes the other in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The Corbie abbot list: Isaac, then Paschasius Radbertus 843-851, then Odo 851-860

stops.name: Corbie, the school passes to Ratramnus
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no charter dates the appointment, some sources tie it to Paschasius's elevation and give 844, others leave it undated, and it is shown here at the year of that elevation
stops.campa: With Paschasius raised to abbot, the teaching of the monastic school is understood to pass to Ratramnus, who has been a master here for years already. The subject is grammar, scripture, and the fathers. The method is the one he will use on every question ever put to him: assemble the authorities, set them against each other, and see what survives the collision. No charter records the appointment, and the sources that do date it do not agree with each other.
stops.quote: As the study of religion was the principal and only object of Ratramn's devotion to learning, and he cherished an ardent zeal for the truth, there arose no dispute among the Theologians of his time in which he did not enter, either of his own accord, or by the command of those to whose authority he was subject.
stops.quote_source: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, quoted in the Preface to the American Edition of The Book of Ratramn
suggested_refs: The monastic school of Corbie under its ninth-century masters
sources: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, in The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Corbie, the king asks a question
stops.date_confidence: attested: the visit of Charles the Bald and the commission are both placed in 843
stops.campa: Charles the Bald comes to the abbey, and what he takes away from it is a doubt. He is king of the West Franks and will not be crowned emperor for another thirty-two years, long after both monks are dead. Uneasy at what Paschasius has written about the altar, he does what a Carolingian king does with a theological problem: he commissions a second opinion on his own abbot's book, from a monk of the same house. Ratramnus opens by writing the question back to him in the king's own terms.
stops.quote: Your excellent Majesty inquireth, whether the Body and Blood of Christ, which in the Church is taken by the mouth of the faithful, be made so in a mystery or in truth; that is, whether it containeth any hidden thing, which lieth open to the eye of faith alone; or whether without the veil of any mystery, the sight gazeth on that Body outwardly, which the eye of the soul inwardly beholdeth, so that the whole matter standeth forth open and manifest.
stops.quote_source: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. V, in The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, written at royal commission
sources: The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Corbie, figure is defined
stops.date_confidence: undated within the treatise: ordered here by the argument, not by the calendar
stops.campa: He does not begin with the altar. He begins with the word. Before he will say what the sacrament is, he fixes the meaning of figura against veritas, and the definition he lays down governs everything that follows: a figure shows what it means under a covering, and truth shows the thing itself with nothing over it. Two men in one cloister, one Latin vocabulary, one loaf on one altar. Paschasius uses the same two words and reaches the opposite conclusion.
stops.quote: Figure is a certain outshadowing, which exhibiteth what it meaneth under some sort of veil
stops.quote_source: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. VII, The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr
suggested_refs: The paired terms figura and veritas as used by both Corbie treatises
sources: The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Corbie, under the veil of bread and wine
stops.date_confidence: undated within the treatise: ordered here by the argument, not by the calendar
stops.campa: The case turns on refusing a split. He will not say that there is bread here and a body beside it, two things laid together on the same cloth. It is one thing, and it holds two accounts of itself at once: to the senses, wheat and the vine; to faith, the body and the blood. What the eye reports and what the soul receives are not rivals, and the covering over the second is the ordinary condition of a sacrament. On the cloth there is one loaf and one cup, and the whole argument is about what to call them.
stops.quote: under the veil of corporeal bread and corporeal wine, the spiritual Body and the spiritual Blood of Christ do exist. Not that two things co-exist diverse between themselves, namely body and spirit; but one and the same thing hath in one respect the nature of bread and wine, in another is the Body and Blood of Christ.
stops.quote_source: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. XVI (p. 21), The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr
suggested_refs: De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. XVI, cited in older literature under an erroneous section number
sources: The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr, djvu text lines 1225-1251

stops.name: Corbie, bread in its nature
stops.date_confidence: undated within the treatise: ordered here by the argument, not by the calendar
stops.campa: Commenting on Ambrose, he sets down the sentence that will be quoted against Rome for seven hundred years and that gets him, in his own century, no reply at all from the abbot two doors away. In its nature it is bread; sacramentally it is the true body of Christ. The distinction costs him nothing to make and will cost other men their lives to repeat. He is a monk answering a royal letter, and he writes it as evenly as he would gloss a line of grammar.
stops.quote: For in its nature it is bread, but sacramentally it is the true Body of Christ, as the Lord Jesus Himself declareth, 'This is My Body.'
stops.quote_source: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. LVII, The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr
suggested_refs: De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. LVII, Ratramnus in his own voice commenting on Ambrose
sources: The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr, djvu text lines 2310-2317

stops.name: Corbie, not corporeal but spiritual
stops.date_confidence: undated within the treatise: ordered here by the argument, not by the calendar
stops.campa: Pressed to say plainly what the faithful receive, he answers with a pair of denials that one century will read as heresy and another as prophecy: it is truly the body of Christ, and it is not his corporeal body; truly his blood, and not his corporeal blood. Nothing here is to be understood bodily. The flesh born of Mary walked in Judea once, was buried, rose, and sits at the right hand of the Father, and it is not being chewed in a Frankish church on a Sunday morning.
stops.quote: Of a truth it is the Body of Christ, yet not His corporeal, but His spiritual Body; it is the Blood of Christ, yet not His corporeal, but His spiritual Blood. Nought then is to be understood here corporally, but all spiritually.
stops.quote_source: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. LX, The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr
suggested_refs: De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, secs. LIX-LX
sources: The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Corbie, the Gospel sentence he leans on
stops.date_confidence: undated within the treatise: ordered here by the argument, not by the calendar
stops.campa: The whole case rests, at the end, on one line of John's Gospel, quoted twice within a few sections of each other. It comes out of the discourse on the bread of life. The Spirit gives life; the flesh is of no use. From it he argues that a change has been worked inwardly by the power of the Holy Spirit, invisible to the eye and open to faith, and that this change, and not any alteration in the wheat, is what feeds the soul and supplies the substance of eternal life.
stops.quote: It is the Spirit that quickeneth, the flesh profiteth nothing
stops.quote_source: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, secs. LXXX-LXXXI, quoting John 6:63, The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr
suggested_refs: De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, sec. LIV, on the inward change wrought by the Holy Spirit
sources: The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Corbie, two books that never name each other
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the observation is Willemien Otten's, drawn from the texts, which carry no date for their mutual silence
stops.campa: Both treatises carry the same title. Both use figura and veritas. Neither cites the other, neither names its opponent, and no record survives of a scene between the two men in chapter or cloister. What later readers call the Carolingian eucharistic controversy may be two monks answering the same king in the same years without ever admitting on parchment that they are answering each other. Whether they ever had it out aloud in the cloister is not a question the sources can answer.
suggested_refs: Willemien Otten's reframing of the ninth-century eucharistic debate

stops.name: Corbie, word comes from Mainz
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Council of Mainz, 848
stops.campa: A synod at Mainz under Hrabanus Maurus, with Louis the German in the hall, condemns the monk Gottschalk of Orbais for teaching that God predestines the damned as surely as the elect. He is beaten, made to swear he will never come back into East Francia, and sent west under guard to answer to his own metropolitan. Ratramnus is in Picardy, a long way off, and no record places him at Mainz or names him in the acts of the synod that will set the next decade of his writing.
suggested_refs: The Council of Mainz, 848, and Gottschalk's condemnation

stops.name: Corbie, word comes from Quierzy
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Council of Quierzy, 849
stops.campa: At the royal villa of Quierzy, a few days' ride from the abbey, Hincmar of Reims and Charles the Bald strip Gottschalk of his priesthood, have him flogged, and order him held silent at Hautvillers, where lesser abbots beat him further and he is made to burn his own books. He will live nineteen more years in that confinement and go on writing out of it. Ratramnus is not in the room, and nobody has asked him. What he does about it, two years later, is write a book.
suggested_refs: The Council of Quierzy, 849, and the confinement at Hautvillers Abbey

stops.name: Corbie, on the predestination of God
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 850-851, written in response to Eriugena's De Divina Praedestinatione
stops.campa: He writes two books defending double predestination: the elect to salvation, the reprobate to damnation, both foreknown, both fixed. His immediate target is John Scotus Eriugena, whom Hincmar had commissioned to demolish Gottschalk and who overshot so far that bishops on Hincmar's own side recoiled from the result. Ratramnus has almost certainly never met the man in the cell at Hautvillers whose doctrine he is defending, and no source records a message passing between Corbie and Hautvillers in either direction.
stops.quote: The writings that Ratramn published in these discussions, gained for him so great a reputation that King Charles the Bald chose him to be his instructor, as to what he ought to believe concerning predestination and the Eucharist.
stops.quote_source: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, quoted in the Preface to the American Edition of The Book of Ratramn
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, De Praedestinatione Dei, in two books
sources: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, in The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Corbie, three words about the Trinity
stops.date_confidence: attested as a work: the year is fixed by no source and is placed among the predestination writings of the early 850s
stops.campa: Hincmar has accused Gottschalk of tritheism for singing trina deitas, a threefold godhead, and has replaced the phrase in his own churches with summa deitas. Ratramnus assembles a dossier out of the fathers to show that the condemned man's formula is old and orthodox, and sends it against the most powerful archbishop in West Francia. The quarrel is over one line of a hymn sung at the office. Gottschalk is at Hautvillers, three years into his confinement, and cannot answer for himself.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus's patristic dossier on trina deitas against Hincmar's summa deitas

stops.name: Corbie, the councils go on without him
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Third Council of Valence, 855; the assembly of 859 at a villa the chronicles call Savonnieres is reported in conciliar chronologies but its site identification is contested
stops.campa: The dispute outlives every attempt to close it. At Valence the bishops condemn Eriugena's treatise and repudiate the chapters agreed at Quierzy; the town lies that spring in Lothar's middle kingdom and passes to Provence before the year is out. Four years later another assembly tries again for peace, and fails again. Gottschalk is still shut up at Hautvillers. Ratramnus is still in Picardy. Nothing in the record says either man is consulted about the terms.
suggested_refs: The Third Council of Valence, 855, condemning Eriugena's treatise

stops.name: Corbie, on the birth of Christ
stops.date_confidence: undetermined: no source dates the work, the attribution as a reply to Paschasius's De Partu Virginis is hedged as probable, and the date shown is a placeholder within his career
stops.campa: The abbot has written that Mary bore her son without her body opening, the womb sealed before, during, and after. Ratramnus writes on the birth of Christ and takes the other view, that a real birth is a birth. It is the second time he has answered his own superior in a book, and the second time neither book names the other. No source gives the year, and the reading of the work as a reply to Paschasius is hedged in the scholarship as probable rather than certain.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, The Birth of Christ, critical edition by Jose Maria Canal Sanchez-Pagin, 1968

stops.name: Corbie, the abbot lays it down
stops.date_confidence: contested: one account gives the resignation as around 853 after ten years, while the abbey's abbot list gives Paschasius 843-851 with Odo in the chair from 851, and the two cannot both stand
stops.campa: Paschasius resigns the abbacy and withdraws to Saint-Riquier, a day down the Somme. He leaves the school, the fields, the sick, and the guests to another man and goes to be a monk somewhere quieter. The sources will not agree on the year, and they disagree by two years in a direction that leaves no room for both. Nobody records a farewell or a last word between the two men who wrote the two most famous books this house has produced. The library keeps both.
suggested_refs: The abbey of Saint-Riquier, to which Paschasius withdrew

stops.name: Corbie, against Macarius the Irishman
stops.date_confidence: attested as a work, undated: placed among the treatises of the 850s
stops.campa: An Irish master called Macarius Scotus is teaching that there is one soul, universal, in which every human being shares. Ratramnus writes against him for the Augustinian position: each person has a soul of their own, single, particular, not a portion of anything larger. The question sounds dry from outside the schoolroom. If souls are not individual, there is nobody in particular to save, and nobody in particular to answer at judgment for what was done.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, On the Soul, written against Macarius Scotus

stops.name: Corbie, news out of the north
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the northern mission is documented, the route by which its news reached Corbie is not
stops.campa: The abbey has a daughter house in Saxony, Corvey, planted in country the Franks subdued by war a generation earlier, and Saxony is the road to the Danes. Hamburg, the archbishopric founded to convert the north, was burned by Vikings in 845 and joined to Bremen. Ansgar has been preaching at Birka on its lake and bargaining with Danish kings at Hedeby for leave to build churches. Letters and trade goods come back down that road into Picardy, and with them report of who up there is baptized and who is not.
suggested_refs: Corvey Abbey, Corbie's Saxon daughter house, founded 822
The Hamburg-Bremen mission field: Birka and Hedeby

stops.name: Corbie, the book on the soul for the bishop of Beauvais
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Odo I held Beauvais 861-881, so the work falls c. 861-868, and the frequently repeated date of 860 is impossible
stops.campa: Odo governed this abbey for nine years and is now bishop of Beauvais, forty miles to the southwest. Ratramnus sends him a second book on the soul, against the same doctrine of one soul shared out among all. The letter goes from a monk to his own former abbot, which may be why it argues instead of deferring. What it works out is what makes a rational creature a person. The year is not fixed anywhere: Odo holds Beauvais from 861, so the book falls in the last seven years of Ratramnus's life.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, Liber de anima ad Odonem Bellovacensem
sources: French Wikipedia, list of bishops of Beauvais

segments.name: The Letter to the Edge of the World

stops.name: Corbie, a missionary's question arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 863-865, before Rimbert's elevation to Hamburg-Bremen in 865, which rules out the see itself as the letter's origin
stops.campa: Rimbert, working the Scandinavian mission Ansgar built, writes south to Corbie with a problem no council has settled. There are cynocephali reported at the edge of his field, men with the heads of dogs. He needs to know whether they possess reason and descend from Adam, because if they do he is obliged to preach to them and baptize them, and if they do not he is spending the Church's time on animals. Rimbert is not yet archbishop of anywhere. He is a missionary in the field with a practical difficulty, and he puts it to a schoolmaster in Picardy.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis, Patrologia Latina 121, cols. 1153-1156
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis (c. 863-865)

stops.name: Corbie, what the report says they do
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 863-865
stops.campa: He works from the description and declines to argue with it. The dog-headed are said to live in villages rather than wander; to keep herds and till ground; to wear clothing instead of going bare; to hold laws and to punish those who break them; and to cover themselves out of modesty, which is to say they know shame. Ratramnus takes each item as evidence given by a witness he has no way to question further, and weighs it as it stands. What sort of creature does those things?
suggested_refs: The behavioural marks weighed in the Epistola: settlement, clothing, cultivation, law, and shame
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis

stops.name: Corbie, Augustine's rule applied
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 863-865
stops.campa: The test he uses is four centuries old and comes off his own shelf. Augustine, writing at Hippo about rumours of monstrous races at the ends of the earth, had ruled that whatever is rational and mortal descends from Adam, however strange the body carrying it about. Ratramnus takes reason, law, and shame as the visible marks of that rationality. A face is not among the marks. He applies the rule to a report he has no way to check, about a country no one at Corbie has seen.
suggested_refs: Augustine, City of God XVI.8, on whether the monstrous races descend from Adam
sources: Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, chapter 8
Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis

stops.name: Corbie, the Life of Christopher on the table
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 863-865
stops.campa: There is a precedent, and it is not in the fathers. The Church already tells of a dog-headed man out of the eastern legends, a cannibal from the country of the cynocephali who received human speech, then baptism, then a Christian name, and is venerated as Saint Christopher. Ratramnus reaches for the saint's Life as an argument: if one of them has been received into the faith and is prayed to by name, the kind cannot be excluded from it in principle. The precedent is a legend, and he uses it as evidence.
suggested_refs: The Coptic Acts of Bartholomew and the dog-headed convert behind the Christopher legend
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis

stops.name: Corbie, the answer goes north
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 863-865, shown at the end of that range
stops.campa: The conclusion is cautious and it is a yes: beings that show reason, keep law, and feel shame may be counted rational, may be counted human, and are owed preaching and the font rather than dismissal as beasts. He has never seen a cynocephalus and says so plainly. The verdict rests on the fathers, a saint's Life, and a traveller's report of a country he cannot reach. He seals the letter and it goes out through the gate, north toward Saxony and the sea.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis, critical edition by Ernst Ludwig Dummler, 1902
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis (c. 863-865)

segments.name: Against the Greeks, and the End

stops.name: Corbie, Paschasius comes home to die
stops.date_confidence: attested: Paschasius returns to Corbie late in life and dies there in 865
stops.campa: The old abbot comes back from Saint-Riquier to the house he left and dies in it. Forty years of disagreement about what happens on an altar end without a recorded meeting, a letter, or a retraction from either side. The community buries him. Ratramnus, old himself now, stays in the choir, and the two books go on sitting in the same library with the same title on both spines. Whatever passed between the two men at the end, if anything did, no monk of Corbie wrote it down.
suggested_refs: The burial of Paschasius Radbertus at Corbie, 865

stops.name: Corbie, an encyclical out of Constantinople
stops.date_confidence: attested: Photius's Encyclical Letter, 867
stops.campa: Photius, patriarch in a city Ratramnus will never see, sends out an encyclical accusing the Latin church of error: the Filioque added to the Creed, and a list of Western customs he treats as corruptions. Rome and Constantinople have been quarrelling over Photius's own elevation for nine years. The letter circulates west and reaches the Frankish clergy, and a copy of it, or a report of what it says, gets to Corbie and onto the desk of a monk in his late sixties.
suggested_refs: The Encyclical Letter of Patriarch Photius, 867
sources: Standard accounts of the Photian Schism

stops.name: Corbie, against the objections of the Greeks
stops.date_confidence: attested as his last major work; the range given in summaries, 863-867, sits awkwardly against the 867 date of the encyclical it answers, and the conflict is left open
stops.campa: His last book defends the Filioque and the usages of the Roman church against the Greek charges. For the first time in a long career of quarrels his opponent is not a Frank he could reach by messenger. He has argued with his own abbot, with the archbishop of Reims, with an Irish philosopher over predestination and an Irish master over the soul; now with the Greek-speaking half of Christendom, from the same desk. The summaries date the work 863 to 867, which sits badly against an encyclical of 867, and no source resolves it.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, Contra Graecorum Opposita Romanam Ecclesiam Infamantium

stops.name: Corbie, the death of Ratramnus
stops.date_confidence: attested as c. 868: no source gives the day and none gives the month
stops.campa: He dies in the abbey around 868, in his late sixties, the same year Gottschalk dies unreconciled in his cell at Hautvillers, still refusing to sign what Hincmar wants signed. No source records the day. No tomb, no epitaph, no grave marker survives or is described anywhere, and the house he never left cannot say which stone he lies under. What he leaves is a shelf: two books on the soul, two on predestination, one on the birth of Christ, one against the Greeks, one letter about dog-headed men, and the treatise on the body and blood.
stops.quote: It is indeed very strange that we know so little concerning a man who in his time appeared as one of the greatest characters on the literary stage.
stops.quote_source: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, quoted in the Preface to the American Edition of The Book of Ratramn

segments.name: Bertramus, and the Long Afterlife of the Books

stops.name: Vercelli, the book on trial under another man's name
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Council of Vercelli, 1050
stops.campa: Two centuries after his death the treatise on the Eucharist is circulating through Italy attributed to John Scotus Eriugena, the philosopher he had written two books against. Berengar of Tours uses it under that wrong name to argue his own case about the altar, and a council at Vercelli condemns the position. The book is condemned in Lombardy under the wrong author's name, and the right one appears nowhere in the proceedings, because nobody in the hall knows it. He had written it for a Frankish king who wanted a second opinion.
suggested_refs: The Council of Vercelli, 1050, and Berengar of Tours

stops.name: Corbie, the name goes wrong
stops.date_confidence: attested as a scribal corruption of around 1100, corrected in scholarship only in the nineteenth century
stops.campa: A copyist writes Bertramus where the manuscript says Ratramnus, and the slip takes. For seven hundred years the treatise travels under a name its author never carried, is printed under it, is quoted under it in England and in Germany, and is catalogued under it by men who believe Bertram and Ratramn to be two different writers. The book keeps its readers throughout; only the author is mislaid. The Maurist scholars of Saint-Maur are the ones who eventually put the two halves back together.
stops.quote: Ratramn, whom many, by disfiguring his true name, have called Bertram, rendered himself very celebrated among the writers of his age.
stops.quote_source: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, quoted in the Preface to the American Edition of The Book of Ratramn
suggested_refs: The Bertramus corruption in the manuscript transmission of De Corpore et Sanguine Domini
sources: Histoire Litteraire de la France, tome v, p. 333, in The Book of Ratramn (Eng. trans.), archive.org id bookofratramnpri00ratr

stops.name: Cologne, the first printed edition
stops.date_confidence: contested: English sources give 1531 and German sources 1532, and no source consulted names a city or a printer, so the attribution to Cologne is unconfirmed
stops.campa: The treatise is set in type for the first time and enters the sixteenth century as ammunition. Reformers read the Carolingian monk as a witness against transubstantiation from inside the medieval church itself, which is what they need and not at all what he had been doing. Nicholas Ridley reads him at Cambridge in the 1540s and says the book turned him; Ridley persuades Cranmer, and Cranmer credits Ratramnus with deciding him. Both Englishmen are burned in the reign that follows.
suggested_refs: The editio princeps of De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, 1531 or 1532, printer and city unconfirmed
sources: Diarmaid MacCulloch, Thomas Cranmer: A Life (1996)

stops.name: Corbie, the abbey suppressed
stops.date_confidence: attested: suppression in 1790, with the shelling of the church in April and May 1918
stops.campa: The Revolution dissolves the house. Eleven hundred and twenty-nine years of continuous community end by decree, the monks go out of the gate, and the library is carted off in lots. The abbey church survives with its portal and its western towers, and takes shellfire in the spring of 1918 when the front runs through the Somme villages a few miles east. Over two hundred manuscripts from the shelves Ratramnus used are still extant, held now in Amiens, in Paris, and in Saint Petersburg.
suggested_refs: The surviving abbey church of Corbie, damaged by shellfire in 1918

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the Corbie books in the east
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Dubrovsky's collection reaches Saint Petersburg in the years after the Revolution, and the exact accession year is not fixed by the sources consulted
stops.campa: Petr Dubrovsky, a Russian collector working in France through the upheaval, buys and carries east a portion of the dispersed Corbie library, and it is shelved in the imperial collection on the Nevsky Prospekt. Books copied on the Somme by men who sang the same office as Ratramnus are catalogued in Russian, two thousand kilometres from the cloister that made them. They are there still, listed under the collector's name as their provenance rather than under the abbey's.
suggested_refs: The National Library of Russia and the Dubrovsky provenance of Corbie manuscripts

stops.name: Paris, the letter printed in Migne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the text: Patrologia Latina 121, cols. 1153-1156; the Latin series is issued 1844-1855 and the exact year of this volume is not verified here
stops.campa: The letter on the dog-headed men is set in double columns in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 121, four short columns of Latin wedged between other men's works. Fifty years afterward Ernst Dummler edits it critically among the Carolingian correspondence. It survives in very few medieval copies, and no scholarly English translation is easy to come by even now, so readers who want to know what Ratramnus decided about the humanity of strangers get it, mostly, at second hand.
suggested_refs: Patrologia Latina 121, cols. 1153-1156
